unit_label: Module A: International Banking - Correspondent Banking and NRI Accounts

facts.statement: A Non-resident Indian (NRI) is a person resident outside India who is a citizen of India. A Person of Indian Origin (PIO) is a person resident outside India who is a citizen of a country other than Bangladesh or Pakistan (or another country the Central Government specifies) and who was a citizen of India, belonged to a territory that became part of India after 15 August 1947, is a child, grandchild or great-grandchild of such a person or of a citizen of India, or is the foreign-origin spouse of such a person; a PIO includes an Overseas Citizen of India cardholder who is resident outside India.
facts.locator: Q1 and Q2; S03 printed pp. 70-71 agrees

facts.statement: The NRE account is a rupee account for NRIs and PIOs, in savings, current, recurring or fixed deposit form (fixed deposits for one to three years, though banks may accept longer terms). Permissible credits include inward remittances, interest, and transfers from other NRE or FCNR(B) accounts; permissible debits include local disbursements, remittances outside India, transfers to other NRE or FCNR(B) accounts and investments in India. The account is repatriable, and interest is exempt from income tax.
facts.locator: Q3, columns for the NRE account; S03 printed pp. 72-73 agrees

facts.statement: The NRO account is a rupee account that any person resident outside India may open for bona fide rupee transactions, in savings, current, recurring or fixed deposit form with terms as for resident accounts. Credits: inward remittances, legitimate dues in India, transfers from other NRO accounts, and rupee gifts or loans from a resident relative within Liberalised Remittance Scheme limits. Debits: local payments, transfers to other NRO accounts, remittance of current income. It is not repatriable except for current income, but balances of NRIs and PIOs are remittable up to USD 1 million per financial year (April-March), with transfers to an NRE account counted inside that amount. Interest is taxable. It may be held jointly with residents on a former or survivor basis. When a resident Indian becomes a non-resident, the existing resident account is designated an NRO account.
facts.locator: Q3, columns for the NRO account; S03 printed pp. 74-75 agrees

facts.statement: The FCNR(B) account is held in a freely convertible foreign currency, by NRIs and PIOs, in term deposit form only, for not less than one year and not more than five years. It is repatriable.
facts.locator: Q3, columns for the FCNR(B) account; S03 printed p. 75 agrees

facts.statement: An SNRR (Special Non-Resident Rupee) account may be opened by a person resident outside India who has a business interest in India, for permissible transactions in rupees. It is non-interest-bearing, its debits and credits are specific or incidental to the business, its tenure runs with the contract or business, and it is repatriable. An NRO account differs: it has no such tenure limit and is not repatriable except for current income and the USD 1 million facility.
facts.locator: Q6; S03 printed pp. 78-79 agrees on non-interest-bearing and repatriable

facts.statement: Loans in India against NRE or FCNR(B) deposits may be given to the account holder or to third parties, subject to usual margin requirements, but may not be used for relending, agricultural or plantation activities, or investment in real estate. For a third-party loan there must be no direct or indirect foreign exchange consideration for the depositor pledging the deposit. A loan to the account holder may be repaid by adjusting the deposit, by inward remittance or from the holder's NRO balances. Premature withdrawal of a deposit is not available while a loan against it is outstanding. Loans outside India against NRE or FCNR(B) deposits are allowed through branches or correspondents of the bank, subject to margin; they are not permitted against NRO balances.
facts.locator: Q3, rows "Loans in India" and "Loans outside India"; S03 printed pp. 82-83 agrees

facts.statement: An authorised dealer or a housing finance institution approved by the National Housing Bank may give an NRI or PIO a rupee housing loan to acquire residential accommodation in India. The amount, margin and repayment period are the same as for a resident; the loan may not be credited to an NRE, FCNR(B) or NRNR account; it must be fully secured by an equitable mortgage of the property, with a lien on other assets in India if necessary; instalments, interest and charges may be paid by remittance from abroad, from funds in an NRE, FCNR(B), NRNR, NRO or NRSR account, from rental income from the property, or by a relative in India through an account-to-account transfer; the interest rate must conform to RBI and NHB directives.
facts.locator: Section 4; S03 printed p. 83 agrees on the main conditions but omits the relative's transfer

payload.title: NRI or PIO: who counts?
payload.core_explanation_md:
Two labels decide who may open non-resident accounts, and both start with **residence outside India**.

- **NRI**: resident outside India **and** a citizen of India.
- **PIO**: resident outside India, a citizen of another country (not Bangladesh or Pakistan, unless the Government specifies otherwise), but with an Indian link: once an Indian citizen, born in a territory that joined India after 15 August 1947, a child, grandchild or great-grandchild of such a person, or the foreign-origin spouse of one. An **OCI cardholder** resident outside India is included.

So the quick test is: *which passport, and where do you live?* An Indian passport holder living abroad is an NRI. A foreign passport holder with Indian roots is a PIO. An Indian citizen on a short trip abroad is still a resident of India.

payload.title: NRE or NRO: where does the money come from, and can it leave?
payload.core_explanation_md:
Both are rupee accounts. What separates them is the **character of the money**.

- **NRE** holds money that came from abroad (and its interest). It is **fully repatriable**, and interest is exempt from income tax. Open only to NRIs and PIOs.
- **NRO** holds money earned or due in India: legitimate dues, transfers from other NRO accounts, and rupee gifts or loans from a resident relative within the Liberalised Remittance Scheme. It is **not freely repatriable**: only current income can go out, plus balances up to **USD 1 million per financial year** for NRIs and PIOs. Its interest is taxable. Anyone resident outside India can open one.

A useful reflex: money that arrived from abroad goes to NRE; money that grew up in India stays in NRO. When a resident becomes a non-resident, the old resident account is re-designated as an NRO account.

payload.title: The USD 1 million window out of an NRO account
payload.core_explanation_md:
An NRO balance is not repatriable as such. The exception is a yearly allowance:

- **Who**: NRIs and PIOs.
- **How much**: up to **USD 1 million per financial year** (April to March), counted together with their other eligible assets.
- **Which transfers count**: remittances abroad *and* transfers to an NRE account sit inside the same allowance.
- **Conditions**: the conditions in the Remittance of Assets regulations, and tax paid or cleared.

The allowance **resets on 1 April**; it does not carry over. Money above the limit can be sent in a later financial year.

self_check.prompt_text: An NRI has already moved USD 700,000 from an NRO account to abroad this financial year. How much of the allowance is left, and when does a fresh allowance begin?
self_check.expected_takeaway: USD 300,000 is left; a new USD 1 million allowance begins on the next 1 April.

payload.title: FCNR(B) and SNRR: the two specialist accounts
payload.core_explanation_md:
**FCNR(B)**: a **foreign currency** term deposit. Held in a freely convertible currency, for **one to five years**, by NRIs and PIOs only. It is repatriable, and because the deposit is in foreign currency the depositor carries no exchange risk on the principal in that currency.

**SNRR**: a **business** rupee account for a person abroad who has a business interest in India. It carries the name of the business, earns **no interest**, runs only for the life of the contract or business, and is repatriable.

Contrast with NRO, which has no business purpose, no tenure limit, and is not freely repatriable.

payload.title: Borrowing against a non-resident deposit
payload.core_explanation_md:
A non-resident can raise a loan against a deposit instead of breaking it.

- **In India** (against NRE or FCNR(B) deposits): to the depositor or to a third party, at usual margin, with no overall ceiling. The funds may not be used for **relending, agricultural or plantation activity, or real estate investment**.
- **Third-party loans**: the depositor must receive **no foreign exchange consideration**, direct or indirect, for pledging the deposit.
- **Repayment of a loan to the depositor**: by adjusting the deposit, by inward remittance, or out of the depositor's NRO balance.
- **While the loan is live**, the deposit **cannot be withdrawn prematurely**.
- **Outside India**: the bank's foreign branches or correspondents may lend against NRE or FCNR(B) deposits, at usual margin; loans against **NRO** balances abroad are not permitted.

payload.title: A housing loan for an NRI: who lends, how it is secured, how it is repaid
payload.core_explanation_md:
An NRI or PIO may borrow rupees to buy a **home** in India from an authorised dealer bank or a housing finance institution approved by the National Housing Bank.

- **Terms**: the amount, margin and repayment period are the same as for a resident borrower.
- **Disbursal**: the loan may **not be credited to an NRE, FCNR(B) or NRNR account**.
- **Security**: **equitable mortgage** of the property, and a lien on other assets in India if necessary.
- **Repayment**: from abroad by remittance; from an NRE, FCNR(B), NRNR, NRO or NRSR account; from **rental income** from the property; or by a **relative in India** through an account-to-account transfer.
- **Rate**: must conform to RBI and NHB directions.

payload.title: Planning remittances under the USD 1 million allowance
payload.core_explanation_md: Illustrative case: an NRI wants to move money out of an NRO account in one financial year. In April she remits USD 420,000, in September USD 310,000, and in January she asks the bank to remit a further USD 350,000. How much may the bank remit in January, and what happens to the rest?

worked_steps.description: Add what has already gone out this year.
Compare the January request with what is left.

payload.final_answer_with_unit: The bank may remit at most USD 270,000 in January; the USD 80,000 balance can wait for the next financial year's allowance

self_check.prompt_text: If she moved USD 100,000 from the NRO account to her NRE account in the same year, would that change the answer?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Yes: transfers to an NRE account count inside the same USD 1 million, so only USD 170,000 would remain.

payload.stem_md: An NRI has so far this financial year remitted USD 640,000 abroad from an NRO account and transferred USD 90,000 from it to an NRE account (illustrative figures). Under the USD 1 million per financial year allowance, how many US dollars can still be remitted this year?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give a whole number of US dollars.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Transfers to an NRE account count inside the allowance. Used: 640,000 + 90,000 = 730,000. Left: 1,000,000 − 730,000 = 270,000.

worked_solution_steps.description: Add remittances and the NRE transfer, which both use the allowance.

payload.stem_md: Under the FEMA-based definition used by RBI, who is a Non-resident Indian (NRI)?

options.text_md: A citizen of any country who was born in India
options.explanation_md: Birth in India does not by itself make a person an NRI.

options.text_md: A citizen of India who is resident outside India
options.explanation_md: This is the definition: Indian citizen, resident outside India.

options.text_md: A foreign citizen with an Indian grandparent living abroad
options.explanation_md: That describes a Person of Indian Origin (PIO), not an NRI.

options.text_md: An Indian citizen who is on a two-week holiday abroad
options.explanation_md: A person on a short trip remains resident in India.

payload.correct_explanation_md: An NRI is a person resident outside India who is a citizen of India. A foreign citizen with Indian roots is a PIO.

payload.stem_md: A bank customer who is an NRI receives a rupee gift from a resident relative, within Liberalised Remittance Scheme limits. Which account may it be credited to?

options.text_md: NRE account
options.explanation_md: NRE is for funds that came from abroad; a gift from a resident relative is a credit for NRO.

options.text_md: FCNR(B) account
options.explanation_md: FCNR(B) is a foreign currency term deposit, not a rupee account.

options.text_md: SNRR account
options.explanation_md: SNRR is for business transactions.

options.text_md: NRO account
options.explanation_md: Rupee gifts or loans from a resident relative within LRS limits may be credited to the NRO account.

payload.correct_explanation_md: A rupee gift or loan from a resident relative within Liberalised Remittance Scheme limits is a permitted credit to the NRI's NRO account.

payload.stem_md: Which account is opened by a person abroad with a business interest in India, carries the name of the business, and earns no interest?

options.text_md: SNRR account
options.explanation_md: The SNRR account is non-interest-bearing and specific to the business.

options.text_md: NRE account
options.explanation_md: An NRE account earns interest and has no business tie.

options.text_md: NRO account
options.explanation_md: An NRO account earns interest and has no business tie.

options.text_md: FCNR(B) account
options.explanation_md: FCNR(B) is a foreign currency term deposit that earns interest.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The SNRR account is the non-interest-bearing account tied to a specific business and to the contract period.

payload.stem_md: Which statement about a housing loan sanctioned to an NRI for buying a residential home in India is correct?

options.text_md: The loan must first be credited to the borrower's NRE account
options.explanation_md: The loan may not be credited to NRE, FCNR(B) or NRNR accounts.

options.text_md: The loan may be repaid out of rental income from the property bought with it
options.explanation_md: Rental income from the property is one permitted source of repayment.

options.text_md: The loan period may be double that allowed to a resident
options.explanation_md: The period is the same as for a resident.

options.text_md: The loan may be unsecured if the borrower has an NRE deposit
options.explanation_md: The loan must be fully secured by an equitable mortgage of the property.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Rental income from the property is a permitted repayment source. The loan is not credited to NRE/FCNR(B) accounts, is on resident terms and is secured by equitable mortgage.

payload.stem_md: An NRI has taken a loan in India against a fixed deposit held in his NRE account. What is the position on withdrawing that deposit before maturity while the loan is outstanding?

options.text_md: It is allowed freely at any time
options.explanation_md: The loan holds the deposit as security.

options.text_md: It is allowed with RBI approval
options.explanation_md: There is no such route while the loan is outstanding.

options.text_md: It is not available while the loan against the deposit is outstanding
options.explanation_md: Premature withdrawal is not available where loans against the deposit are availed of.

options.text_md: It is allowed up to half the deposit
options.explanation_md: No such partial permission applies.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Where a loan against a deposit is availed of, the facility for premature withdrawal of that deposit is not available.

payload.stem_md: Up to what amount can an NRI or PIO remit abroad out of balances in an NRO account in a financial year, subject to conditions and taxes?

options.explanation_md: USD 250,000 is below the limit.
USD 500,000 is below the limit.

options.text_md: USD 2 million
options.explanation_md: USD 2 million is above the limit.

options.text_md: USD 1 million
options.explanation_md: An NRI or PIO may remit up to USD 1 million a financial year from NRO balances, subject to conditions and taxes.

payload.correct_explanation_md: An NRI or PIO may remit up to USD 1 million a financial year from NRO balances, subject to conditions and taxes.

Income-tax residency tests (printed pp. 69-70: 182-day and 120-day rules, RNOR, deemed resident) are not taught: they are Finance Act matters not checked against Income-tax Act sources.
RFC accounts for returning NRIs (printed p. 77) are not taught: not found in the RBI FAQ used; they need a primary source.
Overseas Corporate Bodies (printed p. 71) are not taught: de-recognised since 2003, little examination weight.
The courseware says NRE term deposits have a minimum of one year; RBI shows one to three years with banks free to accept longer. The items say only one year or more where needed.

The RBI Master Direction page shows an update on 8 Sep 2026, after the 30 June 2026 cut-off, and the FAQ is dated 16 Jan 2025. The housing-loan terms match the 2026 courseware, so they are treated as applicable at the cut-off.
